How Your Loans Cut What You Can Borrow

Every £100 a month you're paying towards loans or cards takes roughly £5,000-£7,000 off what a mortgage lender will offer you. This guide walks through the arithmetic they use, and what you can do about it.

If you have a loan and you're hoping for a mortgage too, one thing about how lenders think is worth knowing. A lender cares less about how much you owe than about what you pay out each month.

That difference decides how much house you can buy.

The arithmetic lenders actually use

A mortgage lender starts with your income and applies a multiple to it. Then they take off the payments you're already committed to each month. That includes personal loan payments, car finance, credit card minimums, and any other regular credit commitment.

The conversion is rough, because every lender's model is different, but it's honest: every £100 a month of existing credit payments takes somewhere around £5,000 to £7,000 off your maximum mortgage.

So if you're paying £320 a month on car finance, the cost isn't really £320. While the agreement runs, it's a £16,000–£22,000 hole in what a lender will offer you.

Try it both ways. Put your income into the affordability calculator with your current commitments, then again with them at zero. The gap between the two answers is what your existing borrowing is costing you in house.

Why a £2,000 balance can hurt more than a £15,000 one

Here's the part most of us don't expect. Because lenders count the monthly payment rather than the balance, how fast you're repaying something matters more than how much of it is left.

  • A £15,000 loan with three years left, at £440 a month, might cost you £25,000 of borrowing power.
  • A £2,000 loan you're clearing quickly, at £400 a month, costs you almost exactly the same.

The second debt is a seventh of the size, and it does nearly the same damage to your application. It's also far cheaper to remove. Two thousand pounds clears it.

This is why "pay off your smallest expensive debts before you apply" is better advice than "pay off your biggest debt", if the goal is the mortgage. It isn't the same as the advice that minimises your interest bill. The two goals genuinely pull in different directions, and it's worth being clear with yourself about which one you're optimising for.

The income multiple, and the cap you can't argue with

Most UK lenders will offer you roughly four to four-and-a-half times your income, and there's a reason the number clusters there. Under rules set by the Financial Policy Committee, a lender is limited in how much of its new mortgage lending can go above 4.5 times income. Lenders call that ratio loan-to-income. It's a limit on the lender's book rather than a ban on your application. That's why lending above 4.5 times exists but is rationed, and why it tends to go to applicants who are strong in every other respect.

If you're near the multiple, your commitments are the lever you can actually move. You can't argue your way past a cap. You can clear a loan.

Stress testing, and why the rate you are offered is not the rate you are assessed at

Lenders don't check that you can afford the payment at the rate you're being offered. They check that you could still afford it if rates rose. The exact mechanism has changed over the years. The Bank of England withdrew its prescriptive affordability stress test in 2022, but the FCA still requires lenders to assess affordability against future rate rises, and lenders still apply their own stress rate.

Put together, it works like this: your other debt is subtracted from your income, and what's left is tested against a rate higher than the one you'll pay. Both effects compound. Use the payment change forecaster to see what a higher rate does to the payment, and the rate stress test to see what it does to your variable-rate borrowing at the same time.

What to do, in order

  1. List every monthly credit payment. Payments, not balances. Loans, cards, car finance, buy-now-pay-later, overdraft. This total is the number that costs you borrowing power.
  2. Find the worst ratio. For each debt, divide the monthly payment by the balance. The highest number is the debt doing the most damage per pound it would take to clear.
  3. Clear what you can, and close it properly. An account settled but left open can still be counted. Get it closed and confirmed.
  4. Don't open anything new. Not in the six months before you apply, and especially not a car.
  5. Leave the credit card, but empty it. A long-standing account helps your credit file. A balance hurts your affordability. Zero balance, account open, is the best of both.
  6. Then re-run the affordability calculator. The improvement is usually larger than people expect, and seeing it is what makes the discipline stick.

The one trap worth naming

Consolidating your debts into one loan with a longer term lowers your monthly payment, which improves your mortgage affordability on paper. It also increases what you repay overall, and it puts a fresh credit agreement on your file right before you apply. Whether that trade is worth it genuinely depends on your case. We've written it up properly here. But don't treat it as a free improvement. It isn't.
